action_criteria.expected_evidence: Thiamine 24 nmol/L, magnesium 1.3 mg/dL, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, sodium 132 mEq/L, BUN 30 and creatinine 1.3 mg/dL after a week of vomiting; folate 2.2 ng/mL and B12 188 pg/mL with MCV 106; bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL and INR 1.6 (Child-Pugh B, MELD-Na 22); ammonia 68 µmol/L supports but does not grade HE.
action_criteria.label: Core laboratory work-up: blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose, INR, ammonia and CRP, with toxicology where alcohol or drugs are in question; thiamine before treatment, vitamin B12 and folate
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies precipitants; eye-movement signs and ataxia after a week of vomiting in malabsorption require a pre-treatment thiamine level and B12.

action_criteria.rationale: Infection is the commonest precipitant of overt HE and can be occult in cirrhosis; this patient is afebrile with a normal white cell count and no focal source, so the screen is recommended rather than required.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not give dextrose before parenteral thiamine.
Do not under-dose thiamine: oral or low-dose IM thiamine is insufficient for active Wernicke encephalopathy (EFNS 2010).
required_recommendations: Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose, at the Wernicke treatment dose: thiamine 200 mg IV three times daily (EFNS 2010; 500 mg three times daily is an accepted alternative), continued until no further improvement, then oral.
Replace magnesium intravenously (magnesium 1.3 mg/dL), which thiamine-dependent enzymes need.
Replace potassium to 4.0 mmol/L or more, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis.
Rehydrate with IV isotonic fluid after the first thiamine dose, raising sodium by no more than 8 mEq/L in 24 hours, and recheck creatinine.

Identify and treat the precipitants of HE: dehydration, hypokalemia and missed lactulose and rifaximin during a week of vomiting; restart rifaximin 550 mg twice daily once she can take oral medicines.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Treat vomiting with ondansetron once potassium and magnesium are corrected and the QT interval is checked; avoid sedating antiemetics.
Replace folate and vitamin B12 and give a multivitamin; separate calcium carbonate from levothyroxine by 4 hours.
Strict gluten-free diet with dietitian review for celiac disease and cirrhosis.
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with recurrent overt HE, MELD-Na 22 (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Concurrent Wernicke encephalopathy and hepatic encephalopathy in NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD-Na 22) with celiac disease; thiamine 24 nmol/L from 7 days of vomiting and chronic malabsorption; ophthalmoparesis, nystagmus, ataxia mandate Wernicke treatment regardless of MRI.

differential.key_features: Ophthalmoparesis + nystagmus + ataxia + thiamine 24 nmol/L = Wernicke; MRI may confirm but does not exclude when absent.
Symmetric signs with eye-movement findings; MRI shows no infarct.

differential.diagnosis: Celiac-related neurological syndrome (gluten ataxia, peripheral neuropathy)
differential.key_features: Acute onset less typical; treat celiac with strict gluten-free diet regardless.
Afebrile with normal WBC and CRP; the symmetric periaqueductal, medial thalamic and mammillary distribution fits Wernicke encephalopathy.
B12 188 pg/mL with folate 2.2 ng/mL, MCV 106 and reduced vibration sense in the feet; may contribute to the neuropathy and macrocytosis but does not cause ophthalmoparesis.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh B (9: bilirubin 2.4 2, albumin 2.6 3, INR 1.6 1, no ascites 1, HE grade II 2); MELD-Na 22 (creatinine 1.3, bilirubin 2.4, INR 1.6, sodium 132).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Ophthalmoparesis and nystagmus are NEVER features of HE — they point to Wernicke; treat both concurrently.
Wernicke is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is supportive but normal MRI does NOT exclude Wernicke.
Non-alcoholic Wernicke is well-described in celiac disease, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, and chronic malabsorption.
Magnesium is a cofactor for thiamine-dependent enzymes; uncorrected hypomagnesemia can make Wernicke encephalopathy refractory to thiamine.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: concurrent Wernicke encephalopathy (non-alcoholic, from celiac malabsorption + vomiting) and HE; ophthalmoparesis/nystagmus are Wernicke signs incompatible with HE; hypomagnesemia blocks thiamine; MRI confirms periaqueductal + mammillary body signal
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 2 required actions (core labs with thiamine and B12, MRI) + recommended infection screen, EEG and drug check; two simultaneous diagnoses (Wernicke + HE) both requiring active treatment; non-alcoholic Wernicke is easy to miss.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. P. is a 49-year-old woman with NASH cirrhosis, celiac disease, and hypothyroidism who presents after 7 days of severe vomiting and poor oral intake from a gastrointestinal illness. She is brought by a friend who found her ataxic, confused, and unable to walk. On exam, she has ophthalmoparesis (limited upward gaze and bilateral abduction), nystagmus on lateral gaze, truncal and appendicular ataxia, absent lower extremity reflexes, decreased vibration sensation in feet, and confusion with asterixis on prolonged arm extension. She has had one prior HE episode and takes lactulose and rifaximin, but has been unable to keep down her medicines for several days.
